solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Might one introduce you unhappily to pot?

definitions.text: Might one introduce you unhappily to pot?

parts.words: Might one introduce you unhappily to pot?
parts.note: surface reading: someone who leads you into drug-taking, to your regret; setter's reading: someone who puts you into the cooking pot, so you become dinner

explanation.walkthrough: Pot looks like cannabis, and the wording invites a dealer or bad influence; the pot is really a cooking pot, and you are what goes in it.
explanation.definitionFit: A person who eats human flesh would put a victim into the stewpot, which is an unhappy introduction indeed.

clue.text: Rest about to blow on way north

parts.note: CA is short for circa, about

indicators.note: in a down clue, travelling north means reading upwards, so the letters run backwards

parts.note: to pant is to blow hard, breathe heavily

explanation.surface: A short break is about to be blown away on a road heading north.
explanation.walkthrough: Only the breathing word heads upwards in this down entry; the circa abbreviation sits above it unchanged.
explanation.definitionFit: A brief daytime doze is a short period of rest, a light sleep taken in a chair.

clue.text: Strict new head of house expelled from school

parts.note: N is the standard abbreviation for new

indicators.note: someone expelled is thrown out, so one letter is removed from the larger word

parts.note: Harrow is a famous English public school in north-west London

indicators.note: the head of a word is its first letter, so only the opening letter is wanted

parts.note: the opening letter of house

explanation.surface: A strict new head of house has been expelled from the school where he taught.
explanation.walkthrough: The head of house is not a person but one letter, the H dropped from the school's name. Harrow is a well-known English boarding school.
explanation.definitionFit: A narrow interpretation is a strict, tightly limited one, the sense used in phrases like narrow reading.

clue.text: More than one notion of almost perfect society

indicators.note: almost means not quite all, so the final letter is left off

parts.note: ideal means perfect
S is the abbreviation for society

explanation.surface: Someone describes a notion of a society that is nearly perfect.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Of' is a link here, and the definition is the plural phrase at the front.
explanation.definitionFit: A notion is a single thought or concept, so several of them together are plural thoughts or concepts.

clue.text: Silly American cardinal crossing island the wrong way

indicators.note: to cross something here is to straddle it, so the outer letters sit on either side

parts.note: A is a standard abbreviation for American
a cardinal number, such as nine, as opposed to an ordinal

indicators.note: going the wrong way means travelling backwards, so the letters run in reverse

parts.note: IS is the abbreviation for island

explanation.surface: A foolish American churchman wanders across an island in the wrong direction.
explanation.walkthrough: The cardinal is not a churchman but a cardinal number; the island abbreviation turns round and sits between the A and the number.
explanation.definitionFit: Asinine means donkey-like in stupidity, so it is a close synonym for foolish behaviour.

clue.text: Reportedly unfeeling member of Soprano family?

indicators.note: something reported is passed on by word of mouth, so the sound matters rather than spelling

parts.note: callous means unfeeling, and it is said the same way as the singer's surname

explanation.surface: Someone in the Sopranos, the TV mob family, is said to be heartless.
explanation.walkthrough: The Sopranos was a mafia TV drama, but the family here is every opera soprano; Maria Callas was the most famous of them.
explanation.definitionFit: Maria Callas was a celebrated twentieth-century opera singer with a soprano voice, so she belongs to that vocal family.

clue.text: Treat a surly Moo in loving fashion?

indicators.note: to treat material is to process it, so these letters are worked into a new order

parts.note: taken as written: the setter's own name joins the fodder

explanation.surface: Moo, the grumpy setter of this puzzle, should be treated with affection.
explanation.walkthrough: Moo is the setter's pseudonym, so the surface asks you to be kind to a grumpy compiler; the word 'Treat' is the anagram signal.
explanation.definitionFit: Amorous means showing romantic love or desire, so the adverb describes acting with affection and tenderness.

clue.text: Cheers up, being amongst many diplomatic staff

indicators.note: amongst means placed in the middle of others, so one piece goes inside another

parts.note: legion means very numerous, as in their number is legion

indicators.note: in a down clue, going up means reading from the bottom, so the word runs backwards

parts.note: ta is British slang for thanks, which is what cheers also means

explanation.surface: Someone raises a toast while mingling with crowds of embassy staff.
explanation.walkthrough: Cheers is not a toast but a word for thanks; ta is the casual British form, and it flips before slipping inside the word for many.
explanation.definitionFit: A legation is a diplomatic mission below embassy rank, and the word also covers the body of officials sent with it.

clue.text: Cushy job, at home in safe surroundings

indicators.note: surroundings enclose whatever sits within them, so one word wraps around another

parts.note: safe and secure are synonyms
to be in is to be at home

explanation.surface: A comfortable job lets you stay at home in safe, cosy surroundings.
explanation.walkthrough: The 'in' before 'safe' is part of the phrase; the enclosing is signalled by the final word.
explanation.definitionFit: A sinecure is a paid position needing little or no work, which is exactly what an easy, comfortable post means.

clue.text: Male recruit possibly becoming cook's assistant?

indicators.note: possibly means in one of several possible forms, so the letters may be arranged differently

parts.note: M is the abbreviation for male
taken as written

explanation.surface: A new army recruit might end up as the kitchen helper to the cook.
explanation.walkthrough: The kitchen assistant is not a person but an ingredient that helps a dish along; the question mark flags the playful definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Turmeric is a yellow spice used in curries, so it helps a cook flavour and colour food.

clue.text: Formidable woman knocking back no booze

indicators.note: knocking back pushes something backwards, so the letters are read in reverse

parts.note: taken as written
grog is rum and water, or any alcoholic drink

explanation.surface: A fearsome woman is refusing a drink, knocking back no alcohol.
explanation.walkthrough: Knocking back looks like drinking, which fits the booze, but it turns the whole phrase round.
explanation.definitionFit: The Gorgons were snake-haired monsters of Greek myth, so the word is used for a frightening, intimidating female.

clue.text: A priest's the one who did it

parts.note: per means for each, a, as in once a day
P is an abbreviation for priest

explanation.surface: In a whodunnit, the priest turns out to be the culprit.
explanation.walkthrough: The opening letter is not just an article; 'a' means per, as in a pound a head.
explanation.definitionFit: Perp is American police slang, short for perpetrator, the person who committed the crime.

clue.text: Biography of a boxer? It's not much fun

definitions.meaning: first meaning: the life story of a boxer, the breed of dog
second meaning: an idiom for a miserable, hard existence

explanation.walkthrough: The boxer looks like a prizefighter, but it is the dog breed, so its biography is the life of a dog.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom describes a wretched, joyless existence, which is a life that brings little pleasure.

clue.text: To which landlord may raise glass, a little brandy in it?

definitions.text: To which landlord may raise glass, a little brandy in it?

parts.words: To which landlord may raise glass, a little brandy in it
parts.note: surface reading: a pub landlord raising a glass to toast someone; setter's reading: the landlord pushes a glass up against a measuring device on an upturned bottle to dispense a tot

explanation.walkthrough: Raising a glass suggests a toast, but here the glass is literally lifted to the spirit dispenser. In British pubs spirits are poured through a fixed measure clipped to the upturned bottle.
explanation.definitionFit: This device is the trade name for the measuring dispenser fitted to bottles behind a British bar, releasing an exact shot.

clue.text: Syndicate member held in Latin American

indicators.note: something held in is contained within, so the letters lie inside the words that follow

parts.note: the run of letters across the join of these two words

explanation.surface: A member of a crime syndicate has been detained in Latin America.
explanation.walkthrough: The syndicate is not a crime gang: at Lloyd's of London, the insurance market, wealthy private backers who join underwriting syndicates are called Names.
explanation.definitionFit: Lloyd's of London calls its individual investors by this word, each belonging to an insurance syndicate.

clue.text: Teenager Mike breaking pact

indicators.note: breaking smashes something into bits, so the letters are reassembled in a fresh order

parts.note: taken as written
Mike is M in the NATO phonetic alphabet

explanation.surface: A teenage boy called Mike breaks a promise he had made.
explanation.walkthrough: Mike is not a boy's name here but the radio code word for one letter.
explanation.definitionFit: A pact is a formal deal between parties, which is an arrangement both sides accept.

clue.text: Place to go in Paris?

parts.note: surface reading: a tourist destination worth visiting in the French capital; setter's reading: a place to go to the toilet, as found on a French street

explanation.walkthrough: The clue sounds like a travel tip, but 'go' is the euphemism for relieving oneself.
explanation.definitionFit: This French word names a public street urinal for men, once common on Parisian pavements.

clue.text: Fellow auditor a little frightening

parts.note: F is the abbreviation for fellow
an auditor is a hearer, and the ear is what hears
some means a small amount

explanation.surface: A colleague who audits the accounts is a bit scary.
explanation.walkthrough: The auditor is not an accountant: the word comes from Latin for listening, so the organ of hearing fits.
explanation.definitionFit: Fearsome means causing fear or dread, so it is a straightforward synonym for alarming or scary.

clue.text: Somehow even the married can be passionate!

indicators.note: somehow means in some unspecified manner, so the letters can come out in any order

parts.note: taken as written
M is the abbreviation for married

explanation.surface: Surprisingly, even long-married couples can still be full of passion.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The married' reads as husbands and wives, but only the abbreviation joins the other letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Vehement means showing strong feeling or intensity, close in sense to fervent or ardent.

clue.text: Feature of Cockney intellectual, one might say

indicators.note: a Cockney accent drops the opening h sound, so the word is said differently
saying something means voicing it, so what counts is how it is pronounced

parts.note: a highbrow is an intellectual; drop the h as a Cockney does and it sounds like a facial feature

explanation.surface: Someone describes a distinctive trait of a working-class London intellectual.
explanation.walkthrough: Cockney is the accent of working-class East London, famous for dropping h at the start of words.
explanation.definitionFit: A feature is any part of the face, such as the nose or mouth, and the line of hair above the eye is one.

clue.text: Pay court to female, as setter does

parts.note: to woo is to court someone romantically
F is the abbreviation for female

explanation.surface: The crossword setter flirts with a woman, as is the setter's habit.
explanation.walkthrough: The setter is not the puzzle compiler but a dog breed, such as an Irish or English setter, and what a dog does is bark.
explanation.definitionFit: A setter is a gun dog, and the word is the sound a dog makes when it barks.

clue.text: In conversation carefully considers strategies

indicators.note: conversation is spoken, so the word is judged by how it sounds, not how it is spelt

parts.note: to weigh options is to consider them carefully

explanation.surface: During a discussion, someone thinks hard about which plans to adopt.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In conversation' reads as setting the scene, but it is the signal that the considering word is heard, not seen.
explanation.definitionFit: Strategies are methods or approaches for doing something, and the plural answer means the same.

clue.text: Stupid spectator having change of heart

indicators.note: a change of heart swaps the middle, so the central letter is replaced by another

parts.note: a witness is an onlooker, one who sees an event

explanation.surface: A foolish onlooker suddenly decides to see things differently.
explanation.walkthrough: The heart of the onlooker word is its central N; swapping it for L gives the answer, and the crossing letters confirm which replacement is meant.
explanation.definitionFit: Witless means lacking sense or intelligence, so it is a direct synonym for foolish or dim.

clue.text: Run about in garden on vacation

indicators.note: one thing set inside another, so a word sits within the remaining letters
vacation means emptying out, so only the outside letters are left

parts.note: the first and last letters of garden
over means about, as in a row over money

explanation.surface: A child on holiday runs around in the garden.
explanation.walkthrough: Run looks like a verb of motion but means manage; 'on vacation' is not a holiday but an emptying of the garden.
explanation.definitionFit: To run a country or company is to direct and control it, which is what governing involves.

clue.text: Way political party initially exploits position

parts.note: ST is short for street, a way
the African National Congress, South Africa's governing party

indicators.note: initially means at the start, so just the opening letter is taken

parts.note: the first letter of exploits

explanation.surface: A political party is quick to take advantage of its situation.
explanation.walkthrough: The ANC is the African National Congress, a common crossword party alongside Labour and the Tories.
explanation.definitionFit: A stance is an attitude or standpoint taken on an issue, which is a position in the argumentative sense.

clue.text: Turn back European official

indicators.note: going back means retracing the route, so the letters are read from the end

parts.note: to veer is to turn sharply
E is the abbreviation for European

explanation.surface: A European bureaucrat is told to go back the way they came.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Turn back' reads as one phrasal verb, but it splits into a word for turning and the signal to reverse it.
explanation.definitionFit: A reeve was a local magistrate or administrator in medieval England, a chief officer of a town or district.

clue.text: Completely stumped, perhaps more than once

definitions.meaning: second meaning: a cricket dismissal such as stumping, happening once and then again

explanation.walkthrough: Stumped looks like baffled, but it is a way for a cricket batsman to be dismissed, and a dismissed batsman is out; twice gives the phrase.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase is an idiom meaning utter or thorough, as in an out-and-out liar, a total one.

clue.text: Keeling over in German river?

indicators.note: a boat keeling over capsizes and turns upside down, so the word is flipped

parts.note: taken as written
GER is the abbreviation for German

explanation.surface: A boat capsizes on a river in Germany.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface places the river in Germany, but it flows through West Africa; the question mark admits the deception.
explanation.definitionFit: The Niger is the principal river of West Africa, running through Mali, Niger and Nigeria to the Atlantic.

clue.text: Began wordy book about US prison

indicators.note: about means around, so one word is wrapped around another

parts.note: the Oxford English Dictionary, a book made of words
pen is American slang for a penitentiary

explanation.surface: Someone started writing a long-winded book about an American jail.
explanation.walkthrough: Wordy looks like long-winded, but the book is full of words in another sense: it is the great dictionary.
explanation.definitionFit: To open something such as a meeting or a show is to start it, so the past tense means started.

clue.text: Author acquiring suit — of this description?

definitions.note: a colour adjective, pointing back to what the suit might look like

indicators.note: acquiring means taking something in, so one word ends up inside another

parts.note: to author a work is to pen it
to suit is to agree with, as when food agrees with you

explanation.surface: A writer buys a suit, and the clue asks what colour it might be.
explanation.walkthrough: Author and suit look like nouns but are both verbs. The definition is the loose phrase at the end: a suit could be of this colour, hence the question mark.
explanation.definitionFit: The answer is a bright yellowish-green shade like that of garden peas, a colour that could describe a suit.

clue.text: Accommodated in Budapest, a terrific capital

indicators.note: something accommodated in a place is housed within it, so the letters lie inside the words

parts.note: the run of letters spanning the end of the city and the next two words

explanation.surface: Someone stayed in Budapest, praising it as a terrific capital city.
explanation.walkthrough: Capital looks like a city, which Budapest is, but it means wealth; that is the false trail.
explanation.definitionFit: An estate is a person's total property and assets, which is capital in the financial sense.

clue.text: Alienate troublesome sergeant

indicators.note: something troublesome causes disorder, so the letters are thrown into a new arrangement

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A difficult sergeant manages to turn the whole platoon against him.
explanation.walkthrough: Troublesome reads as a description of the soldier, but it is what tells you to rearrange his rank.
explanation.definitionFit: To estrange someone is to make them unfriendly or cut off, which is what alienating means.
